facts.claim: How much lower the body feels on the move for each litre a minute of supplemental oxygen: a climbing climber's felt altitude is the real one less this much per L/min, and their SpO2 and capacity are the felt altitude's. Fitted to the low flows: climbing to the South Col on 2 L/min and on the summit on 3 L/min, SpO2 stayed about 70%, which the saturation curve gives at about 7,260 m: 350 and 530 m a litre; and the roughly 3,000 ft bottled oxygen is said to buy, 300–460 m a litre at those flows.

How much lower the body feels at rest for each litre a minute of supplemental oxygen: breathing slower, a resting climber gets far more of each litre. Fitted so that resting at the South Col on 2 L/min gives the 95% measured there, which the saturation curve gives at about 500 m.

How much of their sea-level capacity, their VO2max, a climber loses for each 1,000 m they feel above the decline's onset, in a straight line. Fitted to the share left at 3,000 m (85%), at 5,000 m (60%) and on the summit (28%): 10% per 1,000 m from 1,500 m leaves 85%, 65% and 27%, where 6% would leave twice as much on the summit.

The rest step's speed, as a share of the steady pace's. Fitted to the spread of each section's hours across the sources, the steady pace taking their middle and the rest step the longest: 4.5 of 6 hours from the South Col to the Balcony, 4 of 5 to the South Summit, 4 of 5 from Camp 3 to the South Col, 1.5 of 2 to the summit, 5 of 7 from Camp 2 to Camp 3.

The faster pace's speed, as a share of the steady pace's. Fitted to the spread of each section's hours across the sources, the steady pace taking their middle and the faster one the shortest: 4.5 against 3 hours from the South Col to the Balcony, 4 against 3 to the South Summit, 4 against 3 from Camp 3 to the South Col, 1.5 against 1 to the summit, 5 against 3 from Camp 2 to Camp 3.

How sure-footed the rest step leaves a climber, against the steady pace (#190): slow, deliberate steps, each foot placed, get back more of the footing ice and a bouncing ladder take. Fitted so that the rest step crosses blue ice and a long ladder that the steady pace slips on.

How sure-footed the faster pace leaves a climber, against the steady pace (#190): hurried steps get back little of what ice and a bouncing ladder take. Fitted so that hurrying across blue ice or a long ladder slips in a few seconds.
How sure-footed a tired climber is, against a fresh one at the same pace (#190): tiredness makes the steps sloppy, and sloppy steps slip.
How sure-footed a profoundly tired climber is, against a fresh one at the same pace (#190).

The litres of water a climber who didn't fill their bottles before setting off is short of from the start (#196): what two one-litre bottles would have given them on the way, less what they drank at Base Camp. Thirst comes sooner, and it tires them faster (body.dehydration-threshold).

The hours on the move a fresh climber, rested, fed and watered, can keep up the steady pace before they're exhausted. Fitted to summit day: away from the South Col at about 22:00 and back by 12:00–14:00, 14–16 hours on the move after a short night, with little food or water, leaves a steady climber tired but able to go on, unless the summit came late.

How fast the rest step tires a climber, as a share of the steady pace's rate. Fitted so that a climber profoundly tired on the summit can still rest-step down to the South Col in the hours the descent usually takes, slower as they are, before they're exhausted.

How fast the faster pace tires a climber, as a share of the steady pace's rate. Fitted so that the faster pace, kept up from the South Col, brings a climber to the summit profoundly tired, with nothing left for the way down: the 10 hours the sections take at a steady pace in the middle of the sources' hours take two-thirds of that, at three times the rate.

The share of their endurance spent at which a climber feels tired. Fitted so that a steady climber who left the South Col at about 22:00 feels it by the time the survivors' median reaches the summit, 09:00–10:00.

The share of their endurance spent at which a climber is profoundly tired, and can only rest-step. Fitted so that a steady climber gets there on the way down when they reached the summit at 13:00–14:00, the median of those who died, and not when they reached it at the survivors' 09:00–10:00: profound fatigue and a late summit are early signs in those who die on the way down.

The hours of rest that take all the fatigue of an exhausted climber away, where the body still recovers: below the death zone, or on oxygen in it. Fitted to the 8–12 hours climbers rest at the South Col, just below the death zone, before the summit push: however tired they arrived, they set off rested, and after the shortest stay, not even tired.

How much endurance a climber loses for each 1% of their body mass in water lost beyond the threshold. Fitted to the 10–11% less work measured at about 3% of body mass lost, 1% past the threshold; the 8% at about 2.4% says the cost comes sooner, which a straight line from the threshold can't follow.
The hours awake after which a climber is short of sleep, and feels it: past them, they've slept six hours or fewer in a day.
How much endurance a climber loses for each day's energy they're short of. Fitted to the 17% by which climbers given carbohydrate at altitude beat those given none, as if a day's energy short.
How short of energy a climber is, in days of what they spend, when they feel hungry: past the shortfall climbers at altitude run every day, eating 50–70% of what they spend.

facts.question: How much lower is a climber's SpO2 while climbing than at rest, at each camp, on air and on oxygen? The model reads the resting values on the move too, and has oxygen alone change with effort.
What is a climber's SpO2 above the Balcony without oxygen, on the South Summit and the summit? The model holds the Balcony's 50% up to the summit.

At 8,000 m, how much faster than a climber's steady pace is the faster one, and how much slower the rest step; and how much more does the faster pace tire them, and how much less the rest step? The model's numbers are fitted to the sections' hours, not measured. Where the footing, not the power, holds a climber back, as on the way down, it tires them as the pace whose power their steps take, in straight lines between the paces and down to nothing standing: is that how it goes?

How many hours of steady climbing can a fresh, acclimatized client keep up above 7,000 m before they're exhausted, on oxygen and without; and how long a rest restores them, in a tent and standing on the ridge?
Does a climber resting above 8,000 m without oxygen grow weaker even at rest, and how fast? The model only stops their recovery there.

How much less does going down tire a climber than going up, at 8,000 m, and how much faster do they go? The model has them walk down as fast as their footing lets them, no faster than the fastest walk, and tires them by the share of their power the steps take, from the energy cost of walking measured near sea level (Minetti et al.): does it hold in crampons, at altitude, with a pack?
How much does a day of eating too little at altitude cost a climber's endurance, and when do they feel it? The model's numbers come from one study of carbohydrate.

How much do a client's sea-level fitness and weight change their speed and endurance on Everest? The model estimates their VO2max from their sex, age, BMI and training (Jackson et al.), no lower than the threshold of independence, and moves them at its share of the typical client's, a 40-year-old of 175 cm and 75 kg who trains 1–3 hours a week, estimated at about 40. It leaves the hours they can keep a pace up as they are, so a less fit client tires more on the same climb only because it takes them longer.
